name: Texture
controls: The surface grain, marks and degradation laid over or built into the graphics: whether surfaces are clean or carry noise, print artifacts, drawn marks, worn edges or screen and signal artifacts, and whether that texture moves.
question: Should surfaces be clean, or carry grain, print marks, hand-drawn marks or screen artifacts?
notes: Texture is the surface pattern; material (its own dimension) is the substance. A flat vector can carry paper grain without implying paper; a chrome object can be perfectly clean. Four kinds of texture matter: physical texture is real, scanned or photographed (a scan of paper, real film grain); visual texture is drawn pattern that implies surface (hatching, stipple, halftone), part of the artwork itself; simulated texture is generated procedurally to mimic the physical (SVG feTurbulence grain, shader noise); animated texture changes over time, either re-rolled every frame (film grain), boiled on twos or threes (hand-drawn line boil), or drifting (dust passing). Animated texture is what separates a living film look from a static filter; a frozen grain layer over moving graphics reads as a dirty screen. Several terms overlap with other dimensions: halftone, risograph and photocopy also appear in material (as whole print processes) and visual style; glitch, VHS and scanlines also appear in effects (as events). Here they mean a persistent surface quality, not a one-off effect. In a HyperFrames build all animated texture must be seek-safe: step an feTurbulence seed attribute on the paused GSAP timeline with a steps() ease, or cycle a set of pre-rendered noise tiles with set() calls; never use unseeded Math.random or requestAnimationFrame loops. Full-frame SVG filters are expensive to render; prefer a 256-512px pre-rendered noise tile repeated as a background image when possible.

options.what: The texture is fixed to the artwork and moves with it; it never re-rolls.
options.prompt: Keep texture static and attached to each object (inside the object's layer, not a full-frame overlay), so it moves, scales and rotates with the object like a printed surface.

options.what: The texture or line is redrawn every 2-3 frames, like hand-drawn animation where each drawing differs slightly.
options.prompt: Boil the texture: prepare 3 variants (different feTurbulence seeds or displacement maps) and cycle them every 2-3 frames at 24 fps (8-12 changes per second) on the timeline with a steps() ease, looping through the set.

options.what: A fresh texture every frame, as with real film grain or signal noise.
options.prompt: Re-roll the texture every frame: tween the feTurbulence seed attribute from 0 to N across the shot with ease steps(N) where N equals frames at 24 fps (or 12 fps for a softer look), or jump the background-position of a large noise tile to a new offset each frame.

options.what: The texture slides slowly across the frame, as dust passing through a projector beam or clouds of noise.
options.prompt: Drift the texture layer slowly across the frame (translate 5-15% of frame width over the shot, linear), independent of the graphics beneath it.

options.what: Texture felt rather than seen, mainly killing digital flatness and gradient banding.
options.prompt: Keep texture at 3-6% opacity; it should be invisible at thumbnail size and only felt full-screen.

options.what: Texture clearly part of the look but never competing with content.
options.prompt: Set texture at 8-12% opacity; clearly visible on flat fields, never reducing text contrast below 4.5:1.

options.what: Texture as a defining stylistic feature, reading at any size.
options.prompt: Push texture to 15-25% opacity or full-strength marks; it is a primary feature of the style. Keep text in clean areas or boost its weight so it remains legible.

options.what: Perfectly smooth digital surfaces with no grain, noise, marks or artifacts.
options.looks: Flat or smoothly shaded fills with razor-sharp edges; gradients render perfectly smooth; looks digital and precise.
options.motion: Nothing on the surface moves independently; all attention goes to shape, type and choreography.
options.use: SaaS product films, UI animation, corporate and Swiss-style brand work, data visualization.
options.vs: Perfectly flat is a material choice (no substance); clean is a texture choice (no surface marks). A glossy 3D object can be clean.
options.prompt: Keep every surface clean: no grain, noise, paper, marks or scanlines. Edges stay crisp at full resolution. If a large gradient bands, fix it with a subtle dither (noise at 2% opacity) rather than visible grain.

options.what: The random, organic speckle of silver halide or dye clouds in photographic film, re-rolled every frame.
options.looks: Fine, soft, irregular luminance speckle across the whole frame, strongest in midtones and shadows; softens digital flatness.
options.motion: The grain is different on every frame, giving the image a subtle shimmer even when nothing moves.
options.use: Cinematic brand films, premium product films, editorial and documentary pieces, grain over gradients in SaaS heroes.
options.conveys: Cinematic warmth, analog authenticity, premium craft.
options.vs: Digital noise is harsher, colored and blocky (sensor or compression); film grain is organic and luminance-based. Print grain is static and on paper; film grain lives in time.
options.prompt: Add film grain as a full-frame overlay: an SVG feTurbulence (type fractalNoise, baseFrequency 0.8-0.95, numOctaves 3) desaturated with feColorMatrix, blended with mix-blend-mode: overlay at 6-10% opacity. Re-roll it at 24 fps by tweening the turbulence seed with ease steps(frames) on the timeline. Grain sits above all graphics and below nothing.

options.what: Harsh, pixel-level random noise in luminance and color, as from a digital sensor at high ISO or TV static.
options.looks: Sharp per-pixel speckle with colored (red/green/blue) specks, flatter and more uniform than film grain; at high levels, TV snow.
options.motion: Re-rolls every frame; can surge in intensity as a transition or glitch accent.
options.use: Tech, cyber and glitch aesthetics, surveillance and data themes, transition accents.
options.conveys: Digital rawness, interference, tension, the machine.
options.vs: Film grain is organic, soft and luminance-only; digital noise is crisp and chromatic. Glitch is structural corruption, not random speckle.
options.prompt: Overlay digital noise: feTurbulence type turbulence at high baseFrequency (1.5-2.5), numOctaves 1, keep color channels (no desaturation), mix-blend-mode: screen at 5-10%. Re-roll every frame via a stepped seed tween. For accents, surge opacity to 40-60% for 3-6 frames during transitions.

options.what: Scattered specks, hairs and particles on film or a lens, appearing and disappearing frame to frame.
options.looks: Small light or dark specks and occasional hairs scattered sparsely over the image; vintage film print.
options.motion: Specks pop in for 1-2 frames at random positions; occasionally a hair lingers for 3-6 frames. Density stays low.
options.use: Vintage and retro films, documentary archival looks, handmade and nostalgic brand pieces.
options.vs: Scratches are long vertical lines from physical damage; dust is small, scattered specks. Dust particles in effects are floating 3D motes in the scene; texture dust sits on the film surface.
options.prompt: Add film dust: prepare 8-12 frames of sparse specks (3-8 small irregular dots and 0-1 thin hair per frame, white or black at 30-60% opacity) as SVG groups or a sprite, and show one at a time, switching every 1-2 frames with timeline set() calls using a fixed pseudo-random order. Keep density sparse: never more than 10 specks visible.

options.what: Thin vertical lines and scuffs from physical damage to film stock running through a projector.
options.looks: One to three fine vertical lines, bright or dark, flickering and drifting slightly sideways; occasional short diagonal scuffs.
options.motion: Lines persist for several frames and jitter horizontally by a pixel or two; they appear and vanish abruptly.
options.use: Vintage, western, horror and archival looks; retro title sequences; grungy brand films.
options.vs: Dust is scattered specks; scratches are lines. Distressed edges wear the edges of shapes; scratches cut across the whole frame.
options.prompt: Overlay 1-3 hairline vertical scratches (1px, white at 25-40% or black at 20%) spanning 40-100% of frame height at fixed positions. Keep each visible for 6-18 frames, jittering x by 1-2px every 2 frames, then cut it and start another elsewhere. Drive all changes as stepped timeline events.

options.what: The fine, irregular surface tooth of paper showing through ink and color.
options.looks: Faint mottled variation in fills and backgrounds, slightly uneven color density; flat color looks printed on stock.
options.motion: Usually static and attached to the page, so it moves with the artwork; sometimes boiled for a hand-made feel.
options.use: Editorial and illustrated explainers, warm SaaS brand films, handmade and paper-cutout styles.
options.vs: Paper (material) is the layered-sheet construction; paper grain is only the surface tooth. Film grain moves every frame; paper grain is static.
options.prompt: Add paper grain: feTurbulence type fractalNoise, baseFrequency 0.6-0.9, numOctaves 4, desaturated, mix-blend-mode: multiply at 5-8% over the background and inside color fills. Keep it static and attached to the page layer (not re-rolled per frame), or boil it on threes if the style is hand-drawn.

options.what: Visible strands and flecks embedded in handmade, recycled or washi paper.
options.looks: Thin curled strands and small flecks scattered through the surface, slightly darker or lighter than the paper.
options.motion: Static and attached to the surface; moves with the page.
options.use: Sustainability and craft brands, Japanese-inspired design, stationery and luxury packaging motion.
options.conveys: Naturalness, craftsmanship, recycled or handmade quality.
options.vs: Paper grain is fine uniform tooth; fibers are discrete visible strands. Felt (material) is fibrous throughout.
options.prompt: Add paper fibers: a static overlay of 30-60 thin curved strands (0.5-1px strokes, 10-40px long, random rotation from a fixed seed) plus small flecks, in a slightly darker tone of the paper at 10-18% opacity, on top of subtle paper grain. Fibers stay fixed to the page.

options.what: Tone rendered as a grid of dots (or lines) whose size varies with value, as in printed reproduction.
options.looks: Regular dot grids at an angle (typically 45 degrees for black), bigger dots in shadows and smaller in highlights; visible at large scale as a graphic pattern.
options.motion: Dot size can animate to fade shapes in and out; dot grids can scale up dramatically as a transition; patterns stay aligned to the screen.
options.use: Pop-art and comic-book styles, editorial and newsprint pieces, retro print, music and streetwear.
options.conveys: Print heritage, pop-art energy, retro graphic punch.
options.vs: Ben-Day dots (strictly) are uniform dots for flat tints in comics; halftone dots vary in size to render continuous tone. Stipple is hand-placed random dots; halftone is a regular grid.
options.prompt: Render tone as halftone: a radial-gradient dot pattern (background-size 6-10px, 45-degree rotation) masked by the shape's luminance, or an SVG pattern whose dot radius is driven by value. Use one ink color on paper. To reveal, tween dot radius from 0 to full over 500ms with power2.out. Dot pitch stays constant regardless of object scale.

options.what: Uneven ink density and speckle from printing on paper: slightly patchy fills and soft, broken edges.
options.looks: Flat colors with mottled density, tiny white voids where ink skipped, slightly soft edges; looks physically printed.
options.motion: Static and attached to the artwork; can boil on threes for a stop-motion print look.
options.use: Editorial illustration, textured vector explainers, retro and print-inspired brand motion.
options.vs: Paper grain is the paper's surface; print grain is imperfection in the ink layer. Risograph texture is a specific, heavier print grain with registration shift.
options.prompt: Add print grain inside every color fill: mask each fill with thresholded fractal noise (feTurbulence baseFrequency 1.2, then feComponentTransfer discrete table) so 3-8% of the fill drops out as tiny voids, and add density mottling (multiply noise at 6%). Edges get a 1px roughness via feDisplacementMap scale 1.5. Static, or boil on threes.

options.what: The coarse speckled grain, uneven coverage and slight registration offsets typical of risograph prints.
options.looks: Grainy, speckled color fills with visible dot noise, light banding, colors slightly offset from each other; bright spot inks.
options.motion: Commonly boiled at 8-12 fps; registration offsets jitter by a pixel.
options.use: Indie brands, zines, event promos, illustrated explainers, music and culture.
options.vs: Risograph ink (material) is the full translucent overprint system; risograph texture is just the grain and offset overlay, and can be added to any palette. Print grain is subtler.
options.prompt: Apply risograph texture to fills: heavy speckle mask (thresholded high-frequency noise, 10-15% of pixels dropped), faint horizontal banding (low-frequency noise stretched along x, 5%), and 1-2px registration offset between color layers. Boil the speckle every 3 frames at 24 fps via a stepped seed tween.

options.what: Toner speckle, dark streaks and crushed tones produced by copier machines.
options.looks: Black toner specks in whites, gray streaks and edge darkening, blotchy blacks, high contrast.
options.motion: Re-rolled each frame or every 2 frames, giving a jittery, re-copied flicker.
options.use: Punk and zine styles, collage, protest and street-culture motion, music videos.
options.vs: Photocopy (material) includes the whole threshold conversion; photocopy noise is the speckle and streak overlay. Digital noise is screen-based and colored.
options.prompt: Overlay photocopy noise: black toner speckle (thresholded noise, sparse, 100% black at 3-5% coverage), 1-2 soft gray vertical streaks near edges at 10-15%, and vignette-like edge darkening. Re-roll speckle every 2 frames (12 fps) with a stepped seed tween.

options.what: Ink spreading into paper fibers, softening and feathering edges beyond the intended line.
options.looks: Lines and letterforms with soft, irregular, slightly swollen edges; darker pooled ink at corners and stroke ends.
options.motion: Ink can visibly spread as a reveal: edges bloom outward over 300-600ms, then settle.
options.use: Editorial, literary and calligraphic pieces, Japanese-inspired design, letterpress-style type.
options.vs: Rough edges are dry and jagged; ink bleed is soft and feathered. Marker texture is streaky; ink bleed is about spread.
options.prompt: Apply ink bleed to type and line art: SVG filter chain of feGaussianBlur (stdDeviation 0.8-1.5), feDisplacementMap from high-frequency noise (scale 2-3), then an alpha threshold (feComponentTransfer) so edges feather irregularly. For reveals, tween the blur stdDeviation from 4 down to 1 while opacity rises, as ink soaking in.

options.what: Tone built from many hand-placed dots, dense in shadows and sparse in highlights.
options.looks: Irregular dot clouds that build form and shading; engraving and scientific-illustration quality.
options.motion: Dots can appear progressively to build an image, or scatter and regroup; boiling on threes keeps it alive.
options.use: Editorial and scientific illustration, heritage brands, luxury packaging motion, engraved-portrait styles.
options.vs: Halftone dots sit on a regular grid and vary in size; stipple dots are uniform in size and vary in density with no grid.
options.prompt: Shade forms with stipple: uniform 1-2px dots placed by density (dense in shadows, sparse in highlights), generated once from a fixed seed (Poisson-disc or weighted random) as SVG circles or a canvas pass. No regular grid. Build reveals by showing dots in batches over 600-1000ms.

options.what: Tone and form built from closely spaced parallel lines.
options.looks: Parallel strokes at one angle; spacing and weight control darkness; engraving, pen illustration or technical drawing look.
options.motion: Lines draw on stroke by stroke; hatching can boil slightly; line direction can follow form as objects turn.
options.use: Editorial and technical illustration, heritage and luxury brands, sketchbook and ink styles.
options.vs: Cross-hatching layers two or more directions for darker tones; hatching uses one. Stipple uses dots.
options.prompt: Shade with hatching: an SVG pattern of parallel 1px lines at 45 degrees (spacing 4px for dark, 8px for light) masked to shadow areas; ink color on paper. Keep line direction consistent per object. Draw hatching on progressively (stroke-dashoffset per line group, 30-50ms stagger).

options.what: Layers of hatching at different angles, crossed to build darker tones.
options.looks: One direction in light shadows, two in mid, three or four in deep shadow; engraving and banknote quality at fine scale, comic-ink quality at coarse scale.
options.motion: Layers draw on in sequence as tone deepens; darkness can animate by adding layers.
options.use: Editorial, comic and graphic-novel styles, heritage brands, dramatic ink explainers.
options.vs: Hatching uses one direction; cross-hatching layers several. Halftone renders tone with dots.
options.prompt: Shade with cross-hatching: layer up to three SVG line patterns (45, -45, 0 degrees, 1px lines, 5px spacing), each masked to a darker tone band, so light shadow gets one layer and deep shadow three. Animate tone changes by drawing in additional layers (stroke-dashoffset, 300ms each).

options.what: Visible painted surface: uneven opaque coverage, brush-direction variation and layered color.
options.looks: Flat-ish color fields with uneven density, visible strokes, slightly broken edges, color variation within fills; gouache or acrylic feel.
options.motion: Fills can paint on with a brush-shaped mask; surface may boil on twos; strokes reveal in direction.
options.use: Editorial and conceptual illustration, cultural and arts brands, warm storytelling explainers.
options.vs: Brush texture is the individual stroke's bristle marks; paint is the whole painted surface. Watercolor is transparent and blooms; paint here is opaque.
options.prompt: Give fills a painted surface: mottled density (multiply fractal noise 8-12%), a directional stroke pattern (stretched noise at 20-30 degrees, 6%), and irregular edges (feDisplacementMap scale 3-5). Reveal fills with a brush-shaped mask sweeping across in 2-3 strokes (clip-path or mask-position tweens, 250ms each).

options.what: Marks left by a brush stroke: bristle striations, dry-brush breakup and tapered ends.
options.looks: Strokes with streaky interiors, broken dry edges and tapered starts and ends; ink-brush or dry-paint look.
options.motion: Strokes write on in the direction they were painted, with speed variation (fast in the middle, slow at the ends).
options.use: Headlines and handwritten type, sports and energetic brands, Asian-calligraphic references, transitions.
options.vs: Paint describes a whole painted area; brush texture is the individual stroke. Marker strokes are uniform with no bristle breakup.
options.prompt: Render strokes with brush texture: a mask of streaky bristle lines along the stroke direction (noise stretched along the path) and dry-brush breakup at the tail (thresholded noise increasing toward the end), with tapered start and end widths. Write strokes on along the path (stroke-dashoffset or mask) using power2.inOut so ends are slower than the middle.

options.what: Dry, powdery, broken strokes of chalk or soft pastel on a rough surface.
options.looks: Strokes with speckled, broken interiors where the surface tooth shows through, soft dusty edges; usually light marks on dark boards.
options.motion: Strokes draw on by hand; boiling on twos or threes; occasional dust puff on emphasis.
options.use: Education and explainers, food and cafe brands, sketch-style diagrams, nostalgic classroom themes.
options.vs: Crayon is waxy and denser; pencil is fine and graphite-gray. Chalk is powdery and broken.
options.prompt: Render strokes as chalk: light strokes (#f2f0e8) on a dark board (#23302a) with a speckled breakup mask (thresholded noise so 20-30% of the stroke drops out), soft edges (0.6px blur) and faint board smudges at 5%. Draw on stroke by stroke and boil on threes.

options.what: Waxy, grainy strokes with uneven coverage that catch the paper's tooth.
options.looks: Bright colors with grainy streaks, paper showing through in lines, rough edges, childlike scribble fills.
options.motion: Scribbled fills appear in back-and-forth strokes; boiling on twos; slightly jittery.
options.use: Children's content, playful brands, doodle-style explainers, emotional or naive storytelling.
options.vs: Chalk is powdery and pale; crayon is waxy and saturated. Marker is smooth and streak-free.
options.prompt: Render strokes and fills as crayon: saturated colors with directional grain (noise stretched along the stroke, thresholded so 15-25% of paper shows through), rough edges (feDisplacementMap scale 3), and scribbled back-and-forth fill strokes instead of solid fills. Boil every 2 frames at 24 fps.

options.what: Fine graphite lines and soft shading with paper tooth showing through.
options.looks: Gray graphite lines of varying pressure, light construction lines, soft smudged shading, sketchbook paper.
options.motion: Lines sketch on with construction lines first; boil on twos; shading builds in passes.
options.use: Concept and sketch-style explainers, storyboards, design-process films, architectural pieces.
options.conveys: Thinking in progress, craft, honesty, ideation.
options.vs: Ink lines are solid black and crisp; pencil lines are gray, pressure-variable and grainy. Chalk is broken and powdery.
options.prompt: Render line art as pencil: graphite gray (#4a4a4a) strokes at 0.8-1.5px with pressure variation (varying stroke width or opacity along path), grain via a noise mask (10-15% breakup), light construction lines at 25% opacity drawn first. Shading uses soft hatching. Sketch lines on with stroke-dashoffset, then boil on twos.

options.what: Bold felt-tip strokes with slightly translucent, streaky ink and darker overlaps.
options.looks: Uniform-width bold lines with rounded ends, streaky fills where strokes overlap darker, slight ink pooling at stroke starts.
options.motion: Strokes write on quickly with confident speed; highlighter swipes across text; underlines and circles scribble on for emphasis.
options.use: Annotation and callouts over UI or footage, whiteboard explainers, doodle-style product motion, social content.
options.vs: Brush strokes taper and break; marker strokes keep uniform width. Pencil is gray and fine.
options.prompt: Render annotations as marker: uniform 3-6px strokes with round caps, ink at 85-90% opacity with mix-blend-mode: multiply so overlaps darken, a slightly darker dot at each stroke start. Write strokes on fast (150-300ms per stroke, power1.inOut) via stroke-dashoffset; circles and underlines overshoot their target slightly as a hand would.

options.what: Shape and letter edges made irregular and slightly jagged, as if cut or drawn by hand.
options.looks: Vector shapes with small irregular wobbles along their contours; no perfect circles or straight lines.
options.motion: Edges typically boil (re-roughened every 2-3 frames) so shapes feel hand-drawn and alive.
options.use: Hand-drawn UI, doodle styles, playful brands, illustrated explainers.
options.vs: Distressed edges show wear and loss (chips, gaps); rough edges are only irregular outlines. Ink bleed is soft; rough edges are crisp but uneven.
options.prompt: Roughen all shape edges with an SVG filter: feTurbulence (baseFrequency 0.02-0.04, numOctaves 2) feeding feDisplacementMap at scale 3-6. Boil the edges by stepping the turbulence seed through 3 values every 3 frames at 24 fps with a steps() ease.

options.what: Edges and surfaces with chips, gaps and wear, as if printed from worn blocks or weathered over time.
options.looks: Shapes and type with eroded corners, missing chunks, specks of lost ink inside fills; vintage stamp or worn signage.
options.motion: Usually static; can erode progressively as a reveal or exit.
options.use: Grunge, vintage and Americana styles, sports and streetwear, craft beverage brands.
options.vs: Rough edges are merely irregular; distressed edges show damage and missing material. Scratches cross the whole frame.
options.prompt: Distress shapes and type: mask them with thresholded multi-octave noise concentrated near edges (combine feTurbulence with an edge mask from feMorphology erode) so corners chip and 5-10% of interior specks drop out. Keep it static. For a reveal, tween the threshold so the shape erodes in from nothing over 600ms.

options.what: The degraded look of analog videotape: color bleed, chroma noise, tracking lines, soft resolution and tape wobble.
options.looks: Soft image, colors smearing horizontally beyond edges, horizontal noise bands at the bottom, slight wobble and jitter, washed blacks, timestamp overlays.
options.motion: Constant micro-jitter, occasional tracking glitches rolling vertically, color flickers.
options.use: 80s and 90s nostalgia, music videos, retro brand campaigns, found-footage themes.
options.vs: CRT scanlines are about the display; VHS is about the tape signal. Glitch is digital corruption; VHS is analog degradation.
options.prompt: Apply a VHS texture: slight softness (blur 0.6px), horizontal chroma bleed (duplicate layer tinted red offset +2px and blue -2px, mix-blend-mode: screen, 40%), lifted blacks (#101010 floor), a noisy band 20-40px tall near the bottom, and 1px horizontal jitter every 2-3 frames. Roll a bright tracking bar vertically across the frame once every few seconds (300ms). All changes are stepped timeline events.

options.what: The visible horizontal lines, phosphor glow and curvature of a cathode-ray-tube display.
options.looks: Fine dark horizontal lines across the image, soft glow around bright elements, slight barrel curvature and vignette, optional RGB phosphor mask.
options.motion: Subtle flicker, a slow rolling brighter band, occasional power-on/off collapse to a line.
options.use: Retro gaming and terminal aesthetics, sci-fi UI, 80s and 90s nostalgia, developer tools with retro flavor.
options.vs: VHS is tape degradation; scanlines are the display. Pixelation is resolution reduction with no lines.
options.prompt: Overlay CRT scanlines: repeating-linear-gradient of 1px dark lines every 3px (rgba(0,0,0,0.25)), a soft glow on bright elements (duplicated blurred layer, screen, 30%), a radial vignette darkening corners 25%, and a slow brighter band (10% of frame height, 5% opacity) rolling down over 6-8s. Optional: power-on by scaling a white line from scaleY 0.005 to 1 over 250ms.

options.what: Blocky squares, color banding and smearing from heavily compressed digital images or video.
options.looks: 8x8 or 16x16 blocks, ringing around edges, posterized gradients; in datamoshing, pixels from one shot smear into the next.
options.motion: Blocks flicker and pop; datamosh smears motion vectors across cuts; artifacts surge on transitions.
options.use: Internet-culture and meme aesthetics, glitch art, music videos, critiques of digital media.
options.conveys: Digital decay, internet culture, irony, rawness.
options.vs: Pixelation is uniform downsampling; compression artifacts are uneven blocks and smears. Glitch covers wider corruption (tearing, RGB split).
options.prompt: Suggest compression artifacts: posterize tones (feComponentTransfer discrete, 5-6 steps), overlay a sparse grid of 16px blocks where each block samples a flattened average color (canvas pass or pre-rendered tiles), and add edge ringing (thin offset duplicate at 15%). Surge the block coverage from 0 to 30-50% for 4-8 frames at transitions. True datamosh requires pre-rendered footage.

options.what: Persistent digital corruption as a surface quality: displaced slices, RGB channel offsets and noise bars.
options.looks: Horizontal slices shifted sideways, red/cyan channel separation, blocky color bars, occasional frozen fragments.
options.motion: Irregular bursts: stable for a while, then 2-6 frames of heavy displacement, then stable again; never constant.
options.use: Tech, security and AI themes, cyber and gaming, music, edgy social content.
options.vs: Glitch as an effect (effects dimension) is a one-off event or transition; glitch texture is an ongoing surface state. VHS is analog; glitch is digital.
options.prompt: Apply glitch texture in bursts: every 1.5-3s (fixed schedule on the timeline), for 3-6 frames, slice the frame into 4-8 horizontal bands (clip-path inset copies) and offset each 5-40px on x, split RGB (red copy +3px, cyan copy -3px, screen blend), then snap back clean. Between bursts the frame is clean. Never glitch body text for longer than 4 frames.

options.what: An image reduced to visible square pixels by downsampling, as in low resolution or mosaic censoring.
options.looks: Uniform grid of flat-color squares replacing detail; hard pixel edges; can be partial or full.
options.motion: Pixel size animates as a transition (resolve from blocky to sharp or the reverse); stepped, not smooth.
options.use: Retro gaming references, transitions, censorship or privacy metaphors, digital-to-physical themes.
options.vs: Pixel art is drawn at low resolution on purpose (a style); pixelation is the degradation of a detailed image. Compression artifacts are uneven blocks.
options.prompt: Pixelate by rendering the element to a small canvas (e.g. 1/16 scale) and drawing it back up with image-rendering: pixelated, or with the SVG pixelate filter (feFlood a 1px dot, feTile it at the pixel size, feComposite in with the source, then feMorphology dilate by half the pixel size). Animate pixel size in discrete steps (32, 16, 8, 4, 1px) every 2-3 frames to resolve to sharp; never tween pixel size smoothly.
